lead: A transducer converts one form of energy into another. A sensor converts a physical quantity (pressure, temperature, strain, position, acceleration) into an electrical signal; an actuator such as a solenoid converts an electrical signal into force and motion. Every engine, fuel, flight-control and air data system starts with transducers, and the accuracy of the whole system is set here, before any computer sees the number.
prereq: You need: Ohm's law. The electronics that amplify and digitise these signals are in Avionics electronics.

blocks.text: An active transducer makes its own signal (a thermocouple, a piezoelectric crystal); a passive one changes a resistance, capacitance or inductance and needs an excitation supply (a strain gauge, an RTD, an LVDT). The output may be a voltage, a current, a resistance, a frequency or an AC amplitude and phase.

A solenoid is a coil wound round a movable iron plunger. Current through the coil makes a magnetic field that pulls the plunger in against a return spring. On/off solenoids open fuel shut-off valves and select hydraulic lines; latching solenoids hold their position with no current; proportional solenoids give a force that follows the coil current and are used in pressure-control valves. When the current stops, the coil's stored energy produces a voltage spike, so the driver needs a flyback diode.

blocks.where: F is the pull on the plunger face in N; B is the flux density in the air gap in T; A is the pole-face area in m²; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. The pull rises steeply as the gap closes, because B rises.

blocks.text: Pressure is force per area, in pascals (1 bar = 100 kPa). Absolute pressure is measured against a vacuum, gauge pressure against the local atmosphere and differential pressure between two ports: an altimeter needs absolute static pressure, an airspeed indicator the difference between pitot and static pressure.

items: Bourdon tube: a curved flattened tube that straightens as pressure rises; used for high pressures such as hydraulics.
Capsule and bellows: thin corrugated shells that expand with pressure; an evacuated (aneroid) capsule drives the altimeter.

Diaphragm with strain gauges: pressure bends a thin diaphragm, and gauges bonded to it change resistance. Silicon diaphragms with diffused (piezoresistive) gauges are the usual electronic pressure sensor.
Capacitive: the diaphragm is one plate of a capacitor, and its deflection changes the capacitance.

blocks.text: A resistance temperature detector (RTD) is a platinum wire or film whose resistance rises almost linearly with temperature: RT = R₀(1 + αT), with R₀ = 100 Ω at 0 °C and α = 0.00385 /°C for the common Pt100. It is accurate and stable and suits oil, fuel and air temperatures. A thermistor is a semiconductor bead whose resistance falls steeply and non-linearly with temperature (NTC); it is sensitive but has a narrow range.

A thermocouple is two different metals joined at the hot end. The Seebeck effect gives an emf that depends on the temperature difference between the hot junction and the cold (reference) junction where the wires meet the copper of the instrument. To get the hot temperature, the instrument measures the cold-junction temperature and adds the emf the thermocouple would give at that temperature: cold-junction compensation. Exhaust gas temperature (EGT) is measured with chromel-alumel (type K) thermocouples, several probes round the exhaust wired in parallel to give an average (see Engine instruments: tachometer and EGT). The emf is not exactly proportional to temperature, so real indicators use the type K table.

blocks.where: GF is the gauge factor (about 2 for metal foil); ΔR is the change of resistance and R the unstrained resistance in Ω; ε = ΔL ÷ L is the strain (1 µε = 10⁻⁶).

blocks.text: A strain gauge is a foil grid bonded to a part; when the part stretches, the grid lengthens and its resistance rises. The change is tiny, so gauges sit in a Wheatstone bridge excited by a steady voltage. With four active gauges (two stretched, two compressed) the output is Vout = Vex × ΔR ÷ R, four times one gauge's output, and temperature effects cancel because all four arms change together.

items: Potentiometer: a wiper on a resistive track gives a voltage proportional to angle; simple, but the wiper wears.

Synchro and resolver: rotating transformers. A synchro has three stator windings 120° apart; a resolver has two at 90°, giving outputs proportional to sin θ and cos θ, so θ = arctan(sine output ÷ cosine output). Both are rugged and used on flight-control and engine actuators.

LVDT and RVDT: an AC-excited primary and two secondaries around a movable core (linear) or rotor (rotary). The difference of the secondaries has an amplitude that follows the displacement and a phase that shows its direction, so it needs a phase-sensitive demodulator.
Speed: a variable-reluctance probe facing a toothed wheel gives one pulse per tooth, f = n × N ÷ 60 for n teeth at N rpm; this measures the engine shaft speeds N1 and N2.

Accelerometers: a proof mass on a spring moves by x = m a ÷ k. Piezoelectric types measure vibration (they cannot hold a steady reading); capacitive MEMS types are small and cheap; servo (force-balance) types hold the mass still with a coil and give the most accurate output, for inertial navigation.

examples.question: A diaphragm pressure transducer has four 350 Ω foil gauges with gauge factor 2.0 in a full bridge excited by 10 V. At full-scale pressure, 100 kPa, two gauges see +1000 µε and two see −1000 µε. (a) Find ΔR of each gauge. (b) Find the full-scale bridge output. (c) Find the sensitivity and the output at 35 kPa. (d) What would one active gauge in a quarter bridge give at full scale?
steps: Full bridge: V<sub>out</sub> = V<sub>ex</sub> × ΔR ÷ R = 10 × 0.70 ÷ 350 = 0.020 V = 20 mV.
Sensitivity: 20 mV ÷ 100 kPa = 0.20 mV/kPa. At 35 kPa: 0.20 × 35 = 7.0 mV.
Quarter bridge: V<sub>out</sub> = 10 × (350.70 ÷ 700.70 − 0.5) = 10 × 0.0004995 = 4.995 mV, about a quarter of the full bridge and slightly non-linear.
examples.answer: ΔR = 0.70 Ω; full-scale output 20 mV; 0.20 mV/kPa, so 7.0 mV at 35 kPa; a quarter bridge would give only about 5.0 mV.

examples.question: An EGT thermocouple reads 24.6 mV at the indicator. The cold junction at the indicator terminals is at 40 °C. Take a constant sensitivity of 41 µV/°C for type K. Find the exhaust gas temperature, and say what goes wrong if cold-junction compensation is left out.
steps: The emf measures the difference: ΔT = E ÷ S = 24.6 × 10⁻³ ÷ 41 × 10⁻⁶ = 600 °C.
Compensation adds the cold-junction temperature: T<sub>hot</sub> = 600 + 40 = 640 °C.
Without compensation the indicator would show 600 °C, reading 40 °C low, and the error would change as the nacelle or cockpit warms up.
examples.answer: EGT ≈ 640 °C. Without cold-junction compensation the reading is 40 °C low. (41 µV/°C is a classroom approximation; a real indicator converts with the type K table.)

traps: Calling a solenoid a sensor. It is an actuator, and it needs a flyback diode across its coil.
Saying a thermocouple measures the hot-end temperature directly. It measures a difference, so cold-junction compensation is needed.
Forgetting that LVDT and resolver outputs are AC and need demodulation.
Using a piezoelectric accelerometer for a steady acceleration. It measures only changing (vibration) signals.

quiz.q: Distinguish active and passive transducers with one example each.
quiz.a: Active makes its own signal (thermocouple); passive changes a property and needs excitation (strain gauge, RTD).

quiz.q: Why does a full bridge with four active gauges give a better output than a quarter bridge?
quiz.a: Four gauges give four times the output, the output is linear, and temperature changes that affect all four arms equally cancel.

quiz.q: A Pt100 (α = 0.00385 /°C) measures oil at 120 °C. Find its resistance.
A solenoid gap has B = 0.8 T over a 2 cm² pole face. Find the pull.
A 60-tooth wheel turns at 3000 rpm in front of a speed probe. Find the pulse frequency.
Choose between a potentiometer and an RVDT for a flap position sensor, with reasons.
quiz.a: The RVDT: it has no sliding contact, so it does not wear and survives vibration and temperature; the potentiometer is cheaper and gives DC directly but its wiper wears. The cost of AC excitation and demodulation is worth paying on a flight-control surface.

quiz.q: An EGT gauge reads 15 °C low on a hot day after a long taxi. Suggest the cause.
quiz.a: The cold junction at the indicator has warmed and the cold-junction compensation is faulty or missing, so the instrument under-reads by the rise in reference temperature.

beyond: Not for the exam. Smart sensors now carry their own microcontroller, linearise and temperature-correct themselves and send a digital value on a bus. Fibre Bragg grating sensors measure strain and temperature along a single fibre for structural health monitoring. Search for 'resolver-to-digital converter', 'MEMS pressure sensor' and 'fibre Bragg grating'.

figure.caption: The worked example's pressure transducer: four 350 Ω gauges in a full bridge on 10 V. Opposite arms are strained the same way (R2 and R3 stretched, R1 and R4 compressed), so their changes add and the output is 20 mV at 100 kPa.

spec.aria: A diamond-shaped Wheatstone bridge excited by a 10 volt battery between the top and bottom corners. The four arms are strain gauges: R1 top left compressed to 349.30 ohms, R2 top right stretched to 350.70 ohms, R3 bottom left stretched, R4 bottom right compressed. A voltmeter between the left and right corners reads 20 millivolts at 100 kilopascals. Notes give 7.0 millivolts at 35 kilopascals and 0.20 millivolts per kilopascal.
